extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, chymists, and learned readers (17th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to conduct, report, and judge chymical/experimental claims and philosophical disputes about material principles; emphasizes experimental relations, provenance, clarity, and civility in argument. Useful for evaluating experimental reports and scientific discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present experiments as relations (not mere prescriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: “warn him not to be forward to believe Chymical Experiments when they are set down only by way of Prescriptions, and not of Relations; that is, unless he that delivers them mentions his doing it upon his own particular knowledge, or upon the Relation of some credible person, avowing it upon his own experience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental reports should state whether the author performed the experiment or is reporting a credible witness; present experiments as first‑hand relations (or clearly attributed second‑hand relations) rather than vague prescriptions or recipes with no provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite specific authors/sources for experiments (avoid vague attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: “they would Leave off that Indefinite Way of Vouching the Chymists say this, or the Chymists affirme that, and would rather for each Experiment they alledge name the Author or Authors, upon whose credit they relate it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adducing experimental evidence, name the author(s) or source rather than referring generically to ‘the Chymists’; this enables readers to judge credibility and gives proper credit (and blame) to originators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify experiments before relying on them
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am troubled, I must complain, that even Eminent Writers... have of late suffer'd themselves to be so far impos'd upon, as to Publish and Build upon Chymical Experiments, which questionless they never try'd; for if they had, they would, as well as I, have found them not to be true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not build theory or further claims on experiments you have not tested yourself; independently reproduce or verify critical experimental claims before incorporating them into argument or theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly and avoid obscurity or intentionally enigmatic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “a Person any Thing vers'd in the Writings of Chymists cannot but Discern by their obscure, Ambiguous, and almost Ænigmatical Way of expressing what they pretend to Teach... Ubi palam locuti fumus, ibi nihil diximus.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain experiments and arguments plainly rather than in intentionally obscure or cryptic language; make reporting intelligible to competent readers and avoid reserving explanations only for initiates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish facts from opinions and candidly acknowledge doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: “I observe, that... men would more carefully distinguish those things that they know, from those that they ignore or do but think, and then explicate clearly the things they conceive they understand, acknowledge ingenuously what it is they ignore, and profess so candidly their Doubts...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should separate empirical facts from conjecture, explicitly state what is known versus what is doubtful, and frankly acknowledge ignorance to guide further inquiry rather than conceal uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise experiments and observable phenomena over abstract syllogisms for sensible questions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am not a little pleased to find that you are resolved on this occasion to insist rather on Experiments then Syllogismes... it might seem injurious to our senses... to have recourse to far‑fetched and abstracted Ratiocination... to know what are the sensible ingredients of those sensible things...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For questions about material/sensible phenomena, emphasize experimental evidence and observable phenomena rather than purely dialectical or scholastic reasoning disconnected from sensory data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms (e.g., Principle/Element) before debating
rubrics_metrics.description: “he wished... they would no longer delay his expected satisfaction... and that was to lay down what should be all along understood by the word Principle or Element.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish and agree upon definitions of key terms at the outset of argument or experimental interpretation so participants and readers share the same conceptual framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appeals to authority; let readers judge evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “they would Leave the Reader to Judge of what is fit for him to Believe of what is Deliver'd, whilst they employ not their own great names to Countenance doubtfull Relations...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lend personal prestige or authority in place of evidence; present the data and provenance so readers can assess the merits themselves rather than deferring to an author's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain civility and decorum in disputation
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have endeavoured... that... the Language should be more smooth, and the Expressions more civil... I am not sorry to have this Opportunity of giving an example how to manage even Disputes with Civility... that a man may be a Champion for Truth, without being an Enemy to Civility...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue critically but politely; prefer civil refutation of ideas over personal invective, since civility aids persuasion and preserves constructive discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sceptical method: propose doubts and multiple hypotheses rather than insist on full consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: “his Part being chiefly but to propose Doubts and Scruples, he does enough, if he shews that his Adversaries Arguments are not strongly Concluding... it is allowable for him to propose two or more severall Hypotheses about the same thing... though these wayes be perhaps inconsistent among Themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sceptic's role can be to expose weaknesses in prevailing accounts by raising doubts and suggesting alternate hypotheses; proposing several plausible, even inconsistent, hypotheses can be useful to show uncertainty and stimulate further testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver matters of fact faithfully and preserve records of discourse/experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: “That I have endeavour'd to deliver matters of Fact, so faithfully, that I may... assist the lesse skilful Readers to examine the Chymical Hypothesis... I desir'd not to be idle whilst they were imploy'd, but would if they pleas'd, by writing down in short hand what should be delivered, preserve Discourses that I knew would merit to be lasting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record experimental procedures, observations, and debates accurately and preserve them for others to examine; faithful factual reporting enables verification and lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider broader causal/explanatory factors beyond traditional trinominal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “there are a thousand Phænomena in Nature... which will scarcely be clearly & satisfactorily made out by them that confine themselves to deduce things from Salt, Sulphur and Mercury... without taking much more Notice than they are wont to do, of the Motions and Figures, of the small Parts of Matter, and the other more Catholick and Fruitful affections of Bodies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining material phenomena, consider alternative explanatory factors (e.g., motions, figures, small‑part behavior) beyond entrenched traditional principles; avoid restrictive theoretical commitments that ignore relevant phenomena.
